analytic.title: A Mixed Semantics Model for Schedulability Analysis of Time Petri Nets

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Two semantics, a strong semantics and a weak one, are usually adopted by time Petri nets in different application context. However, both of them are not suitable for the schedulability analysis of real-time systems. The scheduling ability of the strong semantics model is limited because of the constraints of the strong timing, whereas the weak one can not guarantee the timeliness of schedules due to the noncompulsory nature of weak timing. In this paper, we propose a mixed semantics model for time Petri nets that efficiently addresses the problem. In our models, the firability of a transition is not dependent on its conflicting transitions, but on its non-conflicting ones. This not only extends the schedule scope of the model, but also keeps some certain strong timing on choices. Therefore, the mixed semantics model can provide a good support for the schedulability analysis and timing verification of time-critical systems.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Time Petri nets (TPNs) [1], [2] are very useful and rather convenient for modeling and analyzing real-time systems (e.g., command and control systems, embedded systems, real-time e-commerce systems). In TPNs, time intervals are associated with transitions. The semantics of such a time interval is: once a transition t begins enabled, the (dynamic) firing interval of the transition is initialized to its static firing interval. The bounds of the dynamic interval decrease synchronously with time. Transition t can be fired only when the value 0 belongs to its dynamic interval. Firing a transition takes no time. If this or another transition is fired, removing the tokens enabling t, then the interval is disabled. When the upper bound of this firing interval reaches 0, two different semantics are usually adopted [3], [4], [5], [6]: strong semantics and weak semantics. The strong semantics forces a transition to fire when its upper bound decreases to 0. However, this semantics is inconsistent with traditional Petri nets semantics [7], where transitions are never forced to fire. For this reason, the weak semantics was proposed, which allows transitions' upper bounds to be below 0. In this case, this transition will no longer be possible to fire unless it becomes enabled again.

The two semantics are useful in different contexts and thus both of them are pursued. The strong semantics is very suitable for the analysis and verification of real-time systems with rigorous timing constraints or deadline, whereas a limitation of this semantics is that the conflict resolution depends largely on time constraints associated with transitions. Thus, the schedulability analysis using this semantics model is not effective in many cases. Let us consider the example in Fig. 1. A task may be performed by activity A1 (t 1 ) or by two sequential activities A2 and A3 (t 2 and t 3 ). In strong semantics, the activity A1 is never executed because t 1 's earliest firing time 5 is more than t 2 's latest firing time 4. This is not an optimal schedule, because fulfilling A1 takes less time than performing A2 and A3. Therefore, this strong timing greatly narrows the scheduling scope of strong semantics models.

On the contrary with weak semantics, time conditions do not force any transition to fire, and firing decisions are local to the transitions themselves but not time conditions. So, this semantics can "non-deterministically" model choices as tradition Petri nets. As shown in Fig. 1, either t 1 can be fired within [5,6], or t 2 within [3,4]. However, if t 1 or t 2 has not yet been fired before their upper time bounds, then their firabilities will be lost and the schedule will be thus terminated. Therefore, weak semantics models cannot guarantee the timeliness of schedules. The defect is fatal to real-time systems.

In this paper, we present a new mixed semantics model for TPNs to deal with the problems of the schedulability analysis in existing semantics models. In our models, the firability of a transition does not depend on timing constraints of transitions conflicting with itself, but on timing conditions of those transitions that are not in conflict with the transition. The treatment not only greatly loosens the timing restriction on choices and enlarges the scheduling scope of the model, but also avoids a situation in which each branch of a choice structure is disabled because of excessive passing of time. Finally, we compare the expressiveness of the proposed model with the two others (weak and strong semantics models) w.r.t. timed language acceptance.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In section II, we define the syntax of a TPN as well as its formal strong and weak semantics. Section III presents a mixed semantics model and discusses its scheduling ability. In section IV, we conclude the paper.

div.head: IV. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: We have presented a mixed semantics model for the schedulability analysis of time Petri nets. This model keeps a reasonable balance between scheduling ability and strong timing, and thus overcomes the weaknesses of strong and weak semantics. Furthermore, we compare the expressive power of the three semantics models w.r.t. timed language acceptance. The comparison results show that the M-TPN has a medium ability to accept timed languages. So the proposed model is a good compromise between the S-TPN and the W-TPN.

Our future work aims at investigating state class methods for timing analysis of the mixed semantics model. The decidability or undecidability of some important properties (such as reachability, liveness, and boundness) in the model will also be discussed.
